query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Under high‐temperature conditions, differences in surface diffusion rates among constituent elements drive early elemental segregation at nanoparticle surfaces and grain boundaries, leading to phase separation that compromises structural and chemical stability, especially in compositions with low noble‐metal content.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near‐equiatomic solid solution nanoparticles exhibiting a homogeneous, single‐phase microstructure produced by physical or chemical fabrication methods.
generation.intervention: Apply in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping during controlled high-temperature ramps (773–1173 K for catalytic tests and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric tests).
generation.conditions: Testing under controlled inert atmospheres at specified high-temperature regimes, with samples having low noble-metal content to isolate the diffusion-driven instability mechanism.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence of compositional inhomogeneities at surfaces and grain boundaries, leading to the formation of secondary phases.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, atoms with higher surface diffusivity migrate faster than others. This differential diffusion creates local enrichments and depletions that nucleate elemental segregation and phase separation, destabilizing the originally homogeneous solid solution.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline (room-temperature or low-temperature maintained nanoparticles), in situ TEM-EDS will reveal the onset of elemental segregation and formation of secondary phases at high temperatures, observable as the appearance of compositional gradients or distinct phase boundaries.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles maintained at room temperature or at temperatures below the threshold for significant atomic mobility, showing uniform elemental dispersion.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be operative in near-equiatomic multielement nanoparticles with minimal noble-metal content; results may differ for nanoparticles with significantly higher noble-metal proportions or for different size scales where alternative stabilization mechanisms might dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature thresholds and the quantitative impact of the differences in diffusion rates among specific elements are not fully established, nor is it clear how slight variations in noble-metal content might alter the onset or extent of phase separation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: one with the standard low noble-metal content and one with added noble metal (to test the effect of composition on diffusion rates). Subject both sets to in situ TEM-EDS during controlled high-temperature ramps within the specified regimes. Compare elemental distribution evolution with a control sample maintained at low temperature.
measurements: Time-resolved elemental mapping (EDS) to track onset and progression of segregation
Identification of emerging secondary phases via diffraction patterns
Comparison of phase boundary development between the standard and noble-metal-enriched samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant difference in elemental segregation or phase separation is detected between the high-temperature samples and the low-temperature controls (or between the standard and noble-metal-enriched samples) under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that differential surface diffusion drives instability is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted a lot of attention in recent years, due to the unique combinations of structural, physical and chemical properties of these alloys [1] – [3] . HEAs usually form simple structures such as body-centered cubic (BCC) (e.g. TaNbHfZrTi [4] , NbTaVWZr [5] etc.) or face-centered cubic (FCC) (e.g., CoCrCuFeNi [6] , CoCrFeMnNi [7] etc.) solid solutions. The large number of the alloying elements in near-equiatomic proportions result in high configurational entropy in these solid solutions. However, these alloys can decompose to multiple phases upon changing the composition or annealing at different temperatures or a combination of both [8] – [10] . Such a phase decomposition is often the result of the complex interplay of configurational entropy of mixing with the enthalpies of mixing of the constituent elements. Additionally, such multiphase microstructures are more likely to exhibit the desired properties for real engineering applications. Hence, tuning the composition and fractions of phases is critical for achieving the desired properties [10] , [11] .

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), as a novel type of material generally consisting of five or more principle elements, have attracted extensive attention in recent years because of their attractive crystallographic and mechanical properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Although it is anticipated that simple solid solution phases are easier to form rather than the intermetallic compounds or complex-ordered phases due to their high configurational entropy [ [8] , [9] ], only a few HEAs have exactly single and stable solid solution structures, among which CoCrFeNiMn alloy is widely concerned [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. It possesses a single face-center-cubic (fcc) solid solution phase even after a series of thermomechanical processing [ [15] , [16] ] and its constituent elements have more sluggish diffusion compared to other conventional alloys [ [17] ]. These characterizations contribute to excellent mechanical properties with a satisfactory combination between tensile strength and ductility [ [18] , [19] ]. frame.goal: Understand the mechanistic basis that governs whether these nanoparticles preserve their structural and chemical stability under high-temperature catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) service conditions, especially when low noble-metal content is targeted.
frame.limitation: The synthesis–structure–property relationships are poorly established, which limits the evaluation of nanoparticle stability and performance under relevant high-temperature conditions.
constraints: Controlled intervention that isolates the mechanism from competing explanations
Observation predictions must be defined relative to a baseline

prior_attempts: Physical and chemical fabrication routes have produced the nanoparticles but did not establish clear structure–property relationships, leaving the stability mechanisms under high-temperature service unclear.
frame.understanding: The role of high-temperature driven elemental segregation and phase separation kinetics—potentially mediated by differences in surface diffusion rates and thermodynamic driving forces—as the determining factor for whether the nanoparticles maintain a stable homogeneous phase, which in turn affects their catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
